prompt: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\alpha}\frac{d\theta}{5-4\cos\theta}$ (your answer will involve inverse trig functions; you may assume that $0\le\alpha<\pi$). Use your answer to show that $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/3}\frac{d\theta}{5-4\cos\theta}=\frac{2\pi}{9}$.

solutions.title: Half-angle substitution
solutions.body:
Let $I(\alpha)=\displaystyle\int_0^\alpha\frac{d\theta}{5-4\cos\theta}$. With $\cos\theta=2\cos^2\frac\theta2-1$,
$$5-4\cos\theta=9-8\cos^2\tfrac\theta2 .$$
On $[0,\alpha]\subset[0,\pi)$ we have $\cos\frac\theta2>0$, so dividing numerator and denominator by $\cos^2\frac\theta2$ and using $\sec^2=1+\tan^2$,
$$I(\alpha)=\int_0^\alpha\frac{\sec^2\frac\theta2\,d\theta}{9\sec^2\frac\theta2-8}=\int_0^\alpha\frac{\sec^2\frac\theta2\,d\theta}{9\tan^2\frac\theta2+1}.$$
Substitute $x=3\tan\frac\theta2$, so $dx=\frac32\sec^2\frac\theta2\,d\theta$; as $\theta$ goes from $0$ to $\alpha$, $x$ goes from $0$ to $3\tan\frac\alpha2$:
$$I(\alpha)=\frac23\int_0^{3\tan(\alpha/2)}\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\frac23\tan^{-1}\!\Big(3\tan\frac\alpha2\Big).$$

**The special value.** For $\alpha=\frac\pi3$: $\tan\frac\pi6=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, so $3\tan\frac\pi6=\sqrt3$ and $\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\frac\pi3$. Hence
$$\int_0^{\pi/3}\frac{d\theta}{5-4\cos\theta}=\frac23\cdot\frac\pi3=\frac{2\pi}{9}.$$ ∎

prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix with real numbers as entries. Suppose $4A^4+I=0$, where $I$ denotes the identity matrix. Prove that the trace of $A$ (i.e. the sum of the entries on the main diagonal) is an integer.
answer: Every eigenvalue satisfies $4\lambda^4=-1$, so $\lambda=\frac{\pm1\pm i}{2}$; non-real eigenvalues of a real matrix pair up with their conjugates, and each conjugate pair contributes $\pm1$ to the trace.

solutions.title: Eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs
solutions.body:
**Eigenvalues.** If $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ (over $\mathbb C$), then $0=(4A^4+I)v=(4\lambda^4+1)v$, so $4\lambda^4+1=0$, i.e. $\lambda^4=-\frac14$. The solutions are
$$\lambda\in\left\{\tfrac{1+i}{2},\ \tfrac{1-i}{2},\ \tfrac{-1+i}{2},\ \tfrac{-1-i}{2}\right\}$$
(check: $\left(\frac{1+i}{2}\right)^2=\frac i2$ and $\left(\frac i2\right)^2=-\frac14$; the others are obtained by multiplying by $i$ and by taking conjugates).

**Trace.** The trace of $A$ is the sum of the roots of the characteristic polynomial $\chi(t)=\det(tI-A)$, counted with multiplicity, and all these roots are among the four numbers above. Since $\chi$ has real coefficients, a non-real root $\mu$ and its conjugate $\bar\mu$ have the same multiplicity. Let $m_1$ be the multiplicity of $\frac{1+i}2$ (and so of $\frac{1-i}2$) and $m_2$ that of $\frac{-1+i}2$ (and of $\frac{-1-i}2$). Then
$$\operatorname{tr}A=m_1\left(\tfrac{1+i}{2}+\tfrac{1-i}{2}\right)+m_2\left(\tfrac{-1+i}{2}+\tfrac{-1-i}{2}\right)=m_1-m_2\in\mathbb Z .$$ ∎

*Remark.* In particular $n=2(m_1+m_2)$ is even; directly, $4^n(\det A)^4=\det(-I)=(-1)^n$ forces $n$ to be even.

prompt: Consider the initial value problem $y'=y^2-t^2$; $y(0)=0$ (where $y'=dy/dt$). Prove that $\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}y'(t)$ exists, and determine its value.

solutions.title: Substitute $x=y+t$ and trap $x$ between $k'/t$ and $k/t$
solutions.body:
**Substitution.** Put $x=y+t$. Then $x'=y'+1=(x-t)^2-t^2+1$, i.e.
$$x'=x^2-2tx+1=1-x(2t-x),\qquad x(0)=0 .$$
We show $x'(t)\to0$; then $y'(t)=x'(t)-1\to-1$. (Heuristically $x\approx\frac1{2t}$, i.e. $y\approx-t+\frac1{2t}$.)

**Step 1: the solution exists for all $t\ge0$ and $-t<y(t)<0$, i.e. $0<x(t)<t$, for $t>0$.** Work on the maximal interval of existence $[0,T^*)$.

(a) $x>0$: $x'(0)=1>0$, so $x>0$ on some $(0,\varepsilon)$. If $x$ had a first zero $T>0$, then $x>0$ on $(0,T)$ and $x(T)=0$ would force $x'(T)\le0$; but $x'(T)=0-0+1=1$. So $x>0$, i.e. $y>-t$, for $t>0$.

(b) $y<0$: from $y'=y^2-t^2$ we get $y'(0)=0$, $y''=2yy'-2t$ so $y''(0)=0$, and $y'''=2y'^2+2yy''-2$ so $y'''(0)=-2$. By Taylor's theorem $y(t)=-\frac{t^3}{3}+o(t^3)<0$ for small $t>0$. If $y$ had a first zero $T>0$, then $y$ would attain its minimum on $[0,T]$ at some $S\in(0,T)$ with $y(S)<0$ and $y'(S)=0$, i.e. $y(S)^2=S^2$, so $y(S)=-S$ and $x(S)=0$, contradicting (a).

Since $|y(t)|<t$, the solution stays bounded on bounded intervals, so it cannot blow up and $T^*=\infty$.

**Step 2: a monotonicity fact.** For fixed $t>0$ the function $\varphi_t(u)=u(2t-u)$ is increasing on $[0,t]$, and $x'=1-\varphi_t(x)$ with $0<x<t$.

**Step 3: for every $k>\frac12$, $x(t)<\frac kt$ for all large $t$.** Let $h(t)=\frac kt$. Then
$$h'-(h^2-2th+1)=2k-1-\frac{k+k^2}{t^2}>0\qquad\text{for } t\ge t_k$$
(for a suitable $t_k\ge\sqrt k$).
- There is $t_2\ge t_k$ with $x(t_2)<h(t_2)$. Otherwise $\frac kt\le x\le t$ on $[t_k,\infty)$, and by Step 2, $x'\le1-\varphi_t(k/t)=1-2k+\frac{k^2}{t^2}\le\frac{1-2k}{2}<0$ for all large $t$, so $x\to-\infty$, contradicting $x>0$.
- Then $x<h$ on $[t_2,\infty)$: otherwise let $s>t_2$ be the first time with $x(s)=h(s)$. Since $x<h$ on $[t_2,s)$, $(x-h)'(s)\ge0$; but $(x-h)'(s)=\big(h^2-2sh+1\big)-h'(s)<0$. Contradiction.

**Step 4: for every $0<k'<\frac12$, $x(t)>\frac{k'}t$ for all large $t$.** Let $g(t)=\frac{k'}t$; now $g'-(g^2-2tg+1)=2k'-1-\frac{k'+k'^2}{t^2}<0$ for all $t>0$.
- There is $t_3$ with $x(t_3)>g(t_3)$. Otherwise $x\le\frac{k'}t$ for all large $t$, so $\varphi_t(x)\le2tx\le2k'$ and $x'\ge1-2k'>0$; then $x\to\infty$, contradicting $x\le k'/t$.
- Then $x>g$ on $[t_3,\infty)$: at a first time $s>t_3$ with $x(s)=g(s)$ we would need $(x-g)'(s)\le0$, but $(x-g)'(s)=(g^2-2sg+1)-g'(s)>0$.

**Step 5: conclusion.** For all large $t$ we have $\frac{k'}t<x<\frac kt\le t$, so by Step 2
$$1-2k\le1-\varphi_t\!\left(\tfrac kt\right)\le x'(t)\le1-\varphi_t\!\left(\tfrac{k'}t\right)=1-2k'+\frac{k'^2}{t^2}.$$
Hence $1-2k\le\liminf x'\le\limsup x'\le1-2k'$. Letting $k\downarrow\frac12$ and $k'\uparrow\frac12$ gives $\lim_{t\to\infty}x'(t)=0$. Therefore the limit of $y'(t)=x'(t)-1$ exists and
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}y'(t)=-1 .$$

**Answer: $-1$**

prompt:
In the diagram, $l_1=\overline{AB}$, $l_2=\overline{AC}$, $x=\overline{BP}$, and $l=\overline{BC}$, where $\overline{AB}$ indicates the length of $AB$; $P$ is a point of $BC$ and $\theta=\theta(x)$ is the angle $\angle APB$ marked in the diagram. Prove that
$$l_2-l_1=\int_0^l\cos(\theta(x))\,dx .$$
answer: With $y(x)=AP$ one has $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos\theta(x)$, so the integral is $y(l)-y(0)=AC-AB$.

solutions.title: Coordinates
solutions.body:
Put $B=(0,0)$, $C=(l,0)$ and $A=(a,h)$ with $h>0$, so $P=(x,0)$ for $0\le x\le l$. Let
$$y(x)=\overline{AP}=\sqrt{(x-a)^2+h^2}>0 ,$$
a differentiable function of $x$ with $y(0)=l_1$ and $y(l)=l_2$, and
$$y'(x)=\frac{x-a}{\sqrt{(x-a)^2+h^2}} .$$
The angle $\theta=\angle APB$ is the angle at $P$ between the vectors $\overrightarrow{PA}=(a-x,h)$ and $\overrightarrow{PB}$, which points in the direction $(-1,0)$ (for $0<x\le l$). Hence
$$\cos\theta=\frac{(a-x,h)\cdot(-1,0)}{\overline{PA}}=\frac{x-a}{\sqrt{(x-a)^2+h^2}}=y'(x).$$
(At the single point $x=0$ the angle is not defined, which does not affect the integral; the integrand is bounded.) By the fundamental theorem of calculus,
$$\int_0^l\cos\theta(x)\,dx=\int_0^l y'(x)\,dx=y(l)-y(0)=l_2-l_1 .$$ ∎

solutions.title: Law of cosines (official approach)
solutions.body:
Let $y=\overline{AP}$. In triangle $ABP$ the angle at $P$ is $\theta$, and in triangle $APC$ it is $\pi-\theta$; by the law of cosines
$$l_1^2=x^2+y^2-2xy\cos\theta,\qquad l_2^2=(l-x)^2+y^2+2(l-x)y\cos\theta .$$
Subtracting, $l_2^2-l_1^2=l^2-2lx+2ly\cos\theta$, so $2y\cos\theta=\dfrac{l_2^2-l_1^2+2lx-l^2}{l}$. Substituting into the first equation,
$$y^2=l_1^2-x^2+x\,\frac{l_2^2-l_1^2+2lx-l^2}{l}$$
(Stewart's theorem). Differentiate with respect to $x$ ($l,l_1,l_2$ are constants):
$$2y\frac{dy}{dx}=-2x+\frac{l_2^2-l_1^2-l^2}{l}+4x=2x+\frac{l_2^2-l_1^2-l^2}{l}=2y\cos\theta ,$$
where the last equality is the expression for $2y\cos\theta$ found above. Since $y>0$, $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\cos\theta$, and therefore
$$l_2-l_1=y(l)-y(0)=\int_0^l\cos\theta(x)\,dx .$$ ∎

prompt: Two diametrically opposite points $P,Q$ lie on an infinitely long cylinder which has radius $2/\pi$. A piece of string with length $8$ has its ends joined to $P$, is wrapped once round the outside of the cylinder, and then has its midpoint joined to $Q$ (so there is length $4$ of the string on each side of the cylinder). A paint brush is attached to the string so that it can slide along the full length the string. Find the area of the outside surface of the cylinder which can be painted by the brush.

solutions.title: Unroll the cylinder: two ellipses
solutions.body:
The circumference is $2\pi\cdot\frac2\pi=4$. Cut the cylinder along a generator and unroll it into an infinite strip of width $4$; it is convenient to work in the universal cover, the whole plane, with coordinates $(u,v)$: $u$ around the cylinder (taken mod $4$), $v$ along the axis. Put $P$ at $(0,0)$ and $Q$ at $(2,0)$ (and their copies at $u\equiv0$ resp. $u\equiv2 \pmod 4$). Unrolling preserves lengths.

**One strand.** The string consists of two strands of length $4$ from $P$ to $Q$, one on each side. The first strand runs from $P=(0,0)$ to $Q=(2,0)$; the brush can be at a point $X$ of it iff the strand can pass through $X$, i.e. iff
$$|XP|+|XQ|\le4$$
(the shortest path from $P$ through $X$ to $Q$ in the plane is two straight segments). This is the filled ellipse $E_1$ with foci $(0,0)$ and $(2,0)$ and major axis $2a=4$: centre $(1,0)$, $a=2$, $c=1$, $b=\sqrt{a^2-c^2}=\sqrt3$:
$$\frac{(u-1)^2}{4}+\frac{v^2}{3}\le1 .$$
The second strand gives in the same way the ellipse $E_2$ with foci $(0,0)$ and $(-2,0)$, centre $(-1,0)$ — i.e. centre $u\equiv3$ on the cylinder.

**The union.** Each ellipse has width $4$ in the $u$-direction, so the two overlap on the cylinder. Split the cylinder into the half $H_1=\{0\le u\le2\}$ and the half $H_2=\{2\le u\le4\}$. $E_2$ spans $-3\le u\le1$, and its middle part $|u+1|\le1$ covers $H_2$; in $H_1$ it only shows up with its two tips, the points at distance between $1$ and $2$ (in the $u$-direction) from its centre: $0\le u\le1$ (distance $u+1$) and $1\le u\le2$, coming from $u-4\in[-3,-2]$ (distance $3-u$). There $E_1$ is in its middle part, at distance $|u-1|\le1$ from its centre, and $|u-1|\le u+1$ for $0\le u\le1$, $|u-1|\le3-u$ for $1\le u\le2$. An ellipse gets narrower further from its centre, so $E_2\cap H_1\subseteq E_1\cap H_1$. By symmetry the same holds in $H_2$ with the roles swapped. Hence the painted area is
$$2\cdot\operatorname{area}\big(E_1\cap\{|u-1|\le1\}\big)=2\int_{-1}^{1}2\sqrt3\sqrt{1-\frac{w^2}{4}}\,dw=8\sqrt3\int_0^1\sqrt{1-\frac{w^2}{4}}\,dw .$$

**The integral.** With $w=2\sin\phi$, $0\le\phi\le\frac\pi6$:
$$\int_0^1\sqrt{1-\frac{w^2}{4}}\,dw=\int_0^{\pi/6}2\cos^2\phi\,d\phi=\Big[\phi+\tfrac12\sin2\phi\Big]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac\pi6+\frac{\sqrt3}{4}.$$
So the area is
$$8\sqrt3\left(\frac\pi6+\frac{\sqrt3}4\right)=6+\frac{4\pi\sqrt3}{3}\approx13.26 .$$

**Answer: $6+\dfrac{4\sqrt3\,\pi}{3}$**

prompt:
Let $a_n$ ($n\ge1$) be the sequence of numbers defined by the recurrence relation
$$a_1=1,\qquad a_n=a_{n-1}a_1+a_{n-2}a_2+\cdots+a_2a_{n-2}+a_1a_{n-1}$$
(so $a_2=a_1^2=1$, $a_3=2a_1a_2=2$ etc.). Prove that $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty\left(\frac29\right)^na_n=\frac13$.
answer: The partial sums $\beta_N$ satisfy $\beta_{N+1}\le\frac29+\beta_N^2$, so $\beta_N<\frac13$ and the series converges; its sum $\alpha$ satisfies $\alpha=\frac29+\alpha^2$, whose roots are $\frac13,\frac23$, and $\alpha\le\frac13$.

solutions.title: Generating function and a bound on partial sums
solutions.body:
Let $t=\frac29$ and $\beta_N=\sum_{n=1}^N a_nt^n$. All $a_n$ are positive integers.

**The partial sums stay below $\frac13$.** For $N\ge1$,
$$\beta_{N+1}=t+\sum_{n=2}^{N+1}\ \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}a_ka_{n-k}\,t^k t^{n-k}\le t+\beta_N^2 ,$$
because every product $a_kt^k\cdot a_{n-k}t^{n-k}$ on the left has $1\le k,\,n-k\le N$, so it is one of the (non-negative) terms in the expansion of $\beta_N^2=\sum_{j,k\le N}a_jt^ja_kt^k$, each used at most once. Now $\beta_1=\frac29<\frac13$, and if $\beta_N<\frac13$ then $\beta_{N+1}<\frac29+\frac19=\frac13$. By induction $\beta_N<\frac13$ for all $N$.

**The series converges and its sum satisfies a quadratic equation.** The series has positive terms and bounded partial sums, so it converges to some $\alpha\le\frac13$. Multiplying the absolutely convergent series $\alpha=\sum a_nt^n$ by itself (Cauchy product),
$$\alpha^2=\sum_{n\ge2}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}a_ka_{n-k}\Big)t^n=\sum_{n\ge2}a_nt^n=\alpha-t .$$
Hence $\alpha^2-\alpha+\frac29=0$, i.e. $\left(\alpha-\frac13\right)\left(\alpha-\frac23\right)=0$. Since $\alpha\le\frac13$, we get $\alpha=\frac13$:
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty\left(\frac29\right)^na_n=\frac13 .$$ ∎

*Remark.* The $a_n$ are the Catalan numbers $a_n=\frac{1}{n}\binom{2n-2}{n-1}$, with generating function $\sum a_nt^n=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4t}}{2}$; at $t=\frac29$ this is $\frac{1-\frac13}{2}=\frac13$.

prompt:
Two types of domino-like rectangular tiles are available: one with two dots on one half and one dot on the other, written here as $[2\mid1]$, and one with two dots on each half, $[2\mid2]$. (In the original the tiles are drawn with dots; we write $[a\mid b]$ for a tile with $a$ dots on its left half and $b$ dots on its right half.) The first type may be rotated end-to-end to produce a tile of type $[1\mid2]$. Let $A(n)$ be the number of distinct chains of $n$ tiles, placed end-to-end, that may be constructed if abutting ends are required to have the same number of dots.

**Example** $A(2)=5$, since the following five chains of length two, and no others, are allowed:
$$[1\mid2][2\mid1],\quad[1\mid2][2\mid2],\quad[2\mid1][1\mid2],\quad[2\mid2][2\mid1],\quad[2\mid2][2\mid2].$$

(a) Find $A(3)$ and $A(4)$.

(b) Find, with proof, a three-term recurrence formula for $A(n+2)$ in terms of $A(n+1)$ and $A(n)$, for $n=1,2,\dots$, and use it to find $A(10)$.

solutions.title: Count by the right end
solutions.body:
There are three tile positions: $X=[2\mid1]$, $Y=[1\mid2]$, $Z=[2\mid2]$. A chain is a sequence of these in which the right end of each tile equals the left end of the next.

Let $u_n$ be the number of chains of $n$ tiles ending with $1$ dot on the right (last tile $X$), and $v_n$ the number ending with $2$ dots (last tile $Y$ or $Z$). Then $A(n)=u_n+v_n$, and $u_1=1$, $v_1=2$.

A chain of length $n+1$ is a chain of length $n$ followed by a compatible tile:
- after a right end $1$, the next tile must start with $1$: only $Y$, which ends in $2$;
- after a right end $2$, the next tile starts with $2$: $X$ (ends in $1$) or $Z$ (ends in $2$).

Hence
$$u_{n+1}=v_n,\qquad v_{n+1}=u_n+v_n .$$
Therefore $A(n+1)=u_{n+1}+v_{n+1}=u_n+2v_n=A(n)+v_n$, and $v_n=u_{n-1}+v_{n-1}=A(n-1)$ for $n\ge2$. So
$$A(n+2)=A(n+1)+A(n)\qquad(n\ge1).$$
(For $n=1$: $v_2=u_1+v_1=3=A(1)$ as well.)

**(a)** $A(1)=3$, $A(2)=5$, so $A(3)=8$, $A(4)=13$.

**(b)** Continuing: $21,34,55,89,144,233$, so
$$A(10)=233 .$$
(These values agree with a direct computer enumeration of all chains.)

solutions.title: Look at the last tile (official approach)
solutions.body:
Call the positions $X=[2\mid1]$, $Y=[1\mid2]$, $Z=[2\mid2]$. Every chain of length $n+1$ can be extended to a chain of length $n+2$: if it ends with $X$ there is exactly one way (add $Y$); if it ends with $Y$ or $Z$ there are exactly two ways (add $X$ or $Z$). Hence
$$A(n+2)=A(n+1)+\#\{\text{chains of length } n+1 \text{ ending in } Y \text{ or } Z\}.$$
A chain of length $n+1$ ends in $Y$ or $Z$ iff its last tile has a $2$ on the right; removing that tile leaves an arbitrary chain of length $n$, and conversely every chain of length $n$ can be extended in exactly one way by a tile ending in $2$ (by $Y$ after a right end $1$, by $Z$ after a right end $2$). So that number is $A(n)$, and
$$A(n+2)=A(n+1)+A(n),\qquad n\ge1 .$$
With $A(1)=3$, $A(2)=5$: $A(3)=8$, $A(4)=13$, and then $21,34,55,89,144$, so $A(10)=233$.
